The curved treble type is usually described as being in G, with all the holes covered giving A3 and a slackened lip dropping to G; six fingerholes and a thumb hole give the natural scale, and cross-fingering and lip tension give the semitones — in 1738 one player was credited with 27 notes and semitones. The treble has a range of about A3 to A5, the alto about G3 to G5 and the tenor about C3 to D5. The mute cornett has its mouthpiece cut into the body and a narrower bore, so it is quieter and softer in tone; the tenor, whose bore is wide in proportion to its length, sounds more like a cornet.

The fingers cover six fingerholes, and the thumb covers the hole on the back; the pitch is changed by cross-fingering and by adjusting the tension of the lips. With all the holes covered you get a low note, and relaxing the lips drops it a further whole tone. A beginner should first steady the seal of the mouthpiece and the lip tension, then practise opening and closing the holes.

The cornett is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 423.21, traceable to the medieval, Renaissance and Baroque periods, and in use between 1500 and 1650. The body is usually curved, sometimes straight; it is a conical tube with six fingerholes and one thumb hole, sounded by the lips at a cup mouthpiece, with the pitch controlled by the holes and by lip tension. The instrument comes in treble, alto, tenor and bass sizes, forming a family. Professional musicians used it for state and ceremonial music, especially to accompany choral singing, and also in wind ensembles such as the loud wind consort.
木管號琴身多以胡桃木、黃楊木、李木、櫻桃木或梨木製成，彎管外覆薄黑皮革或羊皮紙；: The body of the cornett is usually walnut, boxwood, plum, cherry or pear, and the curved ones are covered with thin black leather or parchment; some are turned from a single piece of wood and bent with steam. The mouthpiece is a separate cup, commonly of horn, ivory or bone, with thread wound round its shank; the socket may carry a brass ferrule, and either end may be bound with silver or brass. Mute cornetts are mostly of boxwood, and straight cornetts show the pale colour of uncovered yellow boxwood. The materials of the other parts are not recorded.
木管號見於中世紀、文藝復興與巴洛克時期，1500至1650年間流行，由職業樂手用: The cornett belongs to the medieval, Renaissance and Baroque periods and was in use between 1500 and 1650, played by professionals for official and ceremonial music, especially to accompany choral singing, and also in loud wind consorts. It was particularly widespread in Germany, because trumpet playing was restricted by the professional trumpeters' guild. The instrument developed in curved and straight forms and as a family of different ranges; the tenor and bass appeared later, and the bass was replaced by the serpent in the seventeenth century. Around 1836 the old name passed to the valved cornet, and the instrument took a new spelling.
木管號見於職業樂手演奏的國家典禮與禮儀音樂，尤其常用於伴奏合唱。它也出現在流行音: The cornett is heard in state ceremonies and ceremonial music played by professionals, and is especially used to accompany choral singing. It also appears in popular music, as a member of the loud wind consort. In Germany it was held in higher regard, because trumpet playing was restricted by the professional trumpeters' guild. The mute cornett has a soft, sweet tone and suits quiet settings; the tenor cornett is often paired with low instruments such as the trombone, filling the lower part.
